name: panic = "abort" in the release profile
baseline: cargo build --release with the default panic = "unwind"
verdict_reason: The Rust Performance Book only says it might increase runtime speed slightly, and no published benchmark gives a number. The measurable effects reported are smaller binaries and slightly faster builds, and it changes program behaviour.
tier_reason: Directional statements only; no runtime numbers in any source found.
claimed_speedup: No numbers: 'might reduce binary size and increase runtime speed slightly' (Rust Performance Book); 'another small reduction in warm build time' (third-party warm-build test)
workload: None published: release builds with panic = "abort" against unwinding
one_liner: Aborting instead of unwinding on panic shrinks binaries; any runtime gain is described as slight and is unmeasured.
how_it_is_fast: With unwinding, the compiler emits landing pads and unwind tables so destructors run while a panic propagates. With abort, a panic ends the process at once, so that code is not generated; the main reported effect is a smaller binary.
use_it_when: Binaries that never catch panics and want smaller output
skip_it_when: Code that uses catch_unwind, or servers that isolate panics per request or thread
Libraries whose users may rely on unwinding
Tests, benchmarks, build scripts and proc macros, which ignore the setting anyway
caveats: No published runtime benchmark found; treat any speed gain as unproven for your program
tradeoffs: Destructors do not run on panic

evidence.quote: This might reduce binary size and increase runtime speed slightly, and may even reduce compile times slightly.
which from my measurements gives another small reduction in warm build time.
Tests, benchmarks, build scripts, and proc macros ignore the panic setting.
